label: lem:HP
title: Lemma
body_md:
\cite{1}\label{lem:HP}
For a linear \([n,k]\) code \(\mathcal C\) with \(0<d_H(\mathcal C)<n\), then
\[
d_H(\mathcal C)+1\le d_p(\mathcal C)\le 2d_H(\mathcal C).
\]
head: environment

label: lem:singleton
title: Lemma
body_md:
\cite{2}\label{lem:singleton}
Let \(\mathcal C\) be a \(q\)-ary code of length \(n\) and minimum symbol-pair distance \(d_p\). Then
\(
|\mathcal C|\le q^{n-d_p+2}.
\)
If \(\mathcal C\) is linear of dimension \(k\), then
\(
d_p\le n-k+2.
\)
head: environment

label: lem:BCH
title: Lemma
body_md:
\cite{MS78}[BCH bound]\label{lem:BCH}
Let \(\mathcal C\) be a cyclic code of length \(n\) over \(\mathbb F_q\) with \(\gcd(n,q)=1\). If its defining set contains
\[
\{b,b+1,\ldots,b+\delta-2\}\subseteq\mathbb Z_n,
\]
then
\(
d_H(\mathcal C)\ge\delta.
\)
head: environment

label: lem:hamming-distance-six
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:hamming-distance-six}
The code $\mathcal{C}_1$ has minimum Hamming distance six.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The five consecutive powers
$
\zeta^{-2},\ \zeta^{-1},\ 1,\ \zeta,\ \zeta^2
$
are roots of $g$. Hence the BCH bound gives
\(
d_{\mathrm H}(\mathcal{C}_1)\ge 6.
\)
To prove the reverse inequality, by \eqref{eq:zeta-relations}, we have $(\zeta^2+\zeta^{-2})^q=\zeta^2+\zeta^{-2}$, so
$\zeta^2+\zeta^{-2}\in\mathbb F_q$. Moreover, $\zeta^2+\zeta^{-2}\ne 0$. Otherwise
$\zeta^4=-1$, and hence $\zeta^8=1$, contradicting
$\operatorname{ord}(\zeta)=n\ge 16$.
The four factors associated with
$\zeta^{-1},\zeta^{-q},\zeta,\zeta^q$ satisfy
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x-\zeta^{-1})(x-\zeta^{-q})
  (x-\zeta)(x-\zeta^q)&=(x-\zeta^{-1})(x+\zeta)
 (x-\zeta)(x+\zeta^{-1})\\
&
=x^4-(\zeta^2+\zeta^{-2})x^2+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Also, the four distinct elements
$1,-1,\zeta^2,\zeta^{-2}$ are roots of $x^{q+1}-1$.
 Therefore,
\[
(x-1)(x+1)(x-\zeta^2)(x-\zeta^{-2})
\mid x^{q+1}-1.
\]
Consequently,
$
g(x)\mid f(x),
$
where
$f(x):=(x^4-(\zeta^2+\zeta^{-2})x^2+1)(x^{q+1}-1).
$
Expanding  $f(x)$ gives
\[
f(x)
=
x^{q+5}-(\zeta^2+\zeta^{-2})x^{q+3}+x^{q+1}-x^4+(\zeta^2+\zeta^{-2})x^2-1.
\]
Since $q\ge 7$, the six exponents
$
0,\ 2,\ 4,\ q+1,\ q+3,\ q+5
$
are distinct and smaller than $n$. All six coefficients
are nonzero. Thus  $f(x)$ represents a codeword of $\mathcal{C}_1$ with
Hamming weight six, and
\(
d_{\mathrm H}(\mathcal{C}_1)\le 6.
\)
This proves the assertion.
head: environment

label: lem:parity-components
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:parity-components}
For  $\mathbf{c}=(c_0,\ldots,c_{n-1})\in \mathcal{C}_1$, define
\[
w_{\mathrm{even}}(\mathbf{c})
=
\bigl|\{j:0\le j\le q,\ c_{2j}\ne 0\}\bigr|
\,\,\, \text{and} \,\,\,
w_{\mathrm{odd}}(\mathbf{c})
=
\bigl|\{j:0\le j\le q,\ c_{2j+1}\ne 0\}\bigr|.
\]
 Then each of $w_{\mathrm{even}}(\mathbf{c})$ and $w_{\mathrm{odd}}(\mathbf{c})$
is either zero or at least four.
In particular, if both parity classes contain nonzero
coordinates, then $w_{\mathrm H}(c)\ge 8$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $m=q+1$ and $\alpha=\zeta^2$, so that $\alpha$ has
order $m$. Write the codeword polynomial uniquely as
$
c(x)=E(x^2)+xO(x^2),
$
where
\[
E(y)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}c_{2j}y^j
\,\,\, \text{and} \,\,\,
O(y)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}c_{2j+1}y^j.
\]

For every
$
t\in\{1,\zeta,\zeta^{-1}\},
$
both $t$ and $-t$ are roots of $g$. Thus,
\[
E(t^2)+tO(t^2)=0
\,\,\, \text{and} \,\,\,
E(t^2)-tO(t^2)=0.
\]
Since the characteristic is odd and $t\ne 0$, these
equations imply
$E(t^2)=O(t^2)=0.$
Consequently,
\[
E(\alpha^{-1})=E(1)=E(\alpha)=0
\,\,\, \text{and} \,\,\,
O(\alpha^{-1})=O(1)=O(\alpha)=0.
\]
The identity $\alpha^q=\alpha^{-1}$ shows that
\[
h(y)=(y-\alpha^{-1})(y-1)(y-\alpha)\in\mathbb F_q[y].
\]
Its three roots are distinct
$m$th roots of unity, so $h(y)\mid y^m-1$.
Both $E$ and $O$ therefore represent words in the
length $m$ cyclic code generated by $h$.

This auxiliary code has three consecutive roots
$\alpha^{-1},1,\alpha$, and hence has minimum Hamming
distance at least four by the BCH bound. It follows that
each of $E$ and $O$ is either zero or has Hamming weight
at least four. Since
$
w_{\mathrm H}(E)=w_{\mathrm{even}}(c),
$ and
$w_{\mathrm H}(O)=w_{\mathrm{odd}}(c),
$
the conclusion follows.
head: environment

label: cor:small-weight-pair
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:small-weight-pair}
If $\mathbf{c}\in \mathcal{C}_1$ has Hamming weight six or seven, then all
its nonzero coordinates lie in one parity class.
Moreover,
\[
w_{ p}(\mathbf{c})=2w_{\mathrm H}(\mathbf{c})\ge 12.
\]
In particular, $C$ contains no codeword of Hamming
weight six with three nonzero cyclic runs.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The assertion about parity follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:parity-components}. Because $n$ is even,
cyclically adjacent coordinates have opposite parity.
Thus no two nonzero coordinates of $c$ are cyclically
adjacent, and each nonzero coordinate forms a separate
nonzero run. Hence
 \[
w_{p}(\mathbf{c})
=
w_{\mathrm H}(\mathbf{c})+\rho(\mathbf{c})
=
2w_{\mathrm H}(\mathbf{c}).
\]
In particular, a codeword of Hamming weight six has
six nonzero runs, rather than three.
head: environment

label: lem:single-run
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:single-run}
If a nonzero codeword of $\mathcal{C}_1$ has a single nonzero cyclic
run and does not have full support, then its Hamming
weight is at least nine.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let the run have length $\ell<n$. Since $\mathcal{C}_1$ is cyclic,
a cyclic shift produces a codeword  $\mathbf{a}\in \mathcal{C}_1$ with
$
\operatorname{supp}(\mathbf{a})=\{0,1,\ldots,\ell-1\},
$
so its polynomial representative satisfies
$
\deg a(x)=\ell-1.
$
Every polynomial representative of a word in $\mathcal{C}_1$ is
divisible by $g(x)$. Since $a(x)\ne 0$, we obtain
$$
\ell-1=\deg (a(x))\ge\deg (g(x))=8.
$$
Hence $\ell\ge 9$.
head: environment

label: thm:mds-pair-distance-ten
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:mds-pair-distance-ten}
For every odd prime power $q\ge 7$, the cyclic code $\mathcal{C}_1$
generated by \eqref{eq:gen-g1} has parameters
$
[n,n-8,6]_q,
$
in the Hamming metric and minimum symbol-pair distance
$
d_{p}(\mathcal{C}_1)=10.
$
Consequently, $\mathcal{C}_1$ is an MDS symbol-pair code.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The dimension calculation and
Lemma~\ref{lem:hamming-distance-six} give the stated
Hamming parameters. Since $\mathcal{C}_1$ is linear, its minimum
symbol-pair distance equals the minimum symbol-pair
weight of its nonzero codewords.

Let $\mathbf{c}\in \mathcal{C}_1$ be nonzero. Then $w_{\mathrm H}(\mathbf{c})\ge 6$.
If $w_{\mathrm H}(\mathbf{c})\in\{6,7\}$,
Corollary~\ref{cor:small-weight-pair} gives
$w_{p}(\mathbf{c})\ge 12.$ If $w_{\mathrm H}(\mathbf{c})=8$, then $c$ does not have full
support because $n\ge 16$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:single-run}, its support cannot consist
of a single nonzero cyclic run. Hence $\rho(\mathbf{c})\ge 2$, and
$$
w_{p}(\mathbf{c})
=
w_{\mathrm H}(\mathbf{c})+\rho(\mathbf{c})
\ge 8+2=10.
$$
If $9\le w_{\mathrm H}(\mathbf{c})<n$, then $\rho(\mathbf{c})\ge 1$,
and therefore
$$
w_{p}(\mathbf{c})\ge w_{\mathrm H}(\mathbf{c})+1\ge 10.
$$
Finally, if $w_{\mathrm H}(\mathbf{c})=n$, then
$
w_{p}(\mathbf{c})=n\ge 16.
$
These cases exhaust all nonzero codewords, proving
$d_{p}(\mathcal{C}_1)\ge 10$.
The Singleton bound for symbol-pair codes states that
\[
|\mathcal{C}_1|\le q^{n-d_{p}(\mathcal{C}_1)+2}.
\]
Since $\dim (\mathcal{C}_1)=n-8$, we have $|\mathcal{C}_1|=q^{n-8}$, and thus
\[
n-8\le n-d_{p}(\mathcal{C}_1)+2.
\]
It follows that $d_{p}(\mathcal{C}_1)\le 10$. Consequently,
$d_{p}(\mathcal{C}_1)=10$, and equality holds in the
symbol-pair Singleton bound.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $q=7$ and write $\mathbb F_{49}=\mathbb F_7(v)$,
where $v^2=-1$. Choose $\zeta=2+3v$, by Magma, $\zeta$ has order $16$.
And the code $\mathcal{C}_1$ has generator polynomial
\[
g_7(x)=x^8+3x^7+3x^6+6x^5+x^3+4x^2+4x+6
\]
and parameters $[16,8,6]_7$ with symbol-pair distance $d_p(\mathcal{C}_1)=10$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $q=11$ and write $\mathbb F_{121}=\mathbb F_{11}(v)$,
where $v^2=-1$. Choose $\zeta=1+3v$, by Magma, $\zeta$ has order $24$.
And the code $\mathcal{C}_1$ has generator polynomial
\[
g_{11}(x)=x^8+5x^7+5x^6+9x^5+2x^3+6x^2+6x+10
\]
and parameters $[24,16,6]_{11}$ with symbol-pair distance $d_p(\mathcal{C}_1)=10$.
head: environment

label: lem:binomial-ratio-revised
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:binomial-ratio-revised}
Let
$
H(y)=ay^r+by^s
$
be a nonzero binomial with distinct exponents
$
0\le r,s\le 2M-1.
$
Assume that
$
H(1)=H(\alpha)=0.
$
Then, after interchanging $r$ and $s$ if necessary,
\[
s=r+M,
\qquad
H(y)=a(y^r-y^{r+M}),
\]
and
\[
H(u)\ne0,\qquad
H(u^3)\ne0,\qquad
\frac{H(u^3)}{H(u)}=\alpha^r\in\mathbb F_q^*.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
From $H(1)=0$ we obtain $b=-a$. Hence
$
0=H(\alpha)=a(\alpha^r-\alpha^s).
$
Since $a\ne0$ and $\alpha$ has order $M$,
$
M\mid(s-r).
$
The exponents lie in the interval $\{0,\ldots,2M-1\}$ and are distinct,
so $|s-r|=M$. After relabeling, $s=r+M$.

Since $u^M=\zeta^{2M}=-1$, we have
$
H(u)=a(u^r-u^{r+M})=2au^r\ne0,
$
and similarly
$
H(u^3)=a(u^{3r}-u^{3r+3M})=2au^{3r}\ne0.
$
Therefore,
\[
\frac{H(u^3)}{H(u)}
=u^{2r}
=\alpha^r\in\mathbb F_q^*.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:trinomial-ratio-revised
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Multiplication by $y^a$ only contributes the factor
\[
\frac{u^{3a}}{u^a}=u^{2a}=\alpha^a
\]
to the quotient. It is therefore enough to consider
$
Q(y)=A_0+A_1y^r+A_2y^s.
$

The exponents $0,r,s$ are pairwise distinct modulo $M$. Indeed, if two
of them were congruent modulo $M$, then the equations
$
Q(1)=Q(\alpha)=0
$
would force the coefficient corresponding to the remaining exponent to
vanish, contrary to the assumption that $Q$ has three nonzero terms.
Since $u^{2r}=\alpha^r$ and $u^{2s}=\alpha^s$, the equations
$
Q(1)=Q(\alpha)=0
$
give
\[
A_1(u^{2r}-1)+A_2(u^{2s}-1)=0.
\]
A direct elimination yields
\[
Q(u)
=
\frac{A_1}{u^{2s}-1}(u^{r}-1)(u^{s}-1)(u^{s}-u^{r}),
\]
and
\[
Q(u^3)
=
\frac{A_1}{u^{2s}-1}
(u^{r}-1)(u^{s}-1)(u^{s}-u^{r})(-u^{r+s}-u^{r}-u^{s}).
\]
The factors in the denominator are nonzero because the three exponents are
distinct modulo $M$, and hence $u^{r},u^{s},1$ are pairwise distinct. Thus
$Q(u)\ne0$ and
\[
\frac{Q(u^3)}{Q(u)}
=-(u^{r+s}+u^{r}+u^{s}).
\]
Restoring the factor $\alpha^a$ proves \eqref{eq:trinomial-ratio-shifted}.

It remains to prove \eqref{eq:trinomial-not-uFq}. Since
\[
u^{qr}=(-1)^ru^{r},\,\,\,
u^{qs}=(-1)^su^{s}\,\,\, \text{and}\,\,\,
u^{q(r+s)}=(-1)^{r+s}u^{r+s},
\]
we consider the parity of $r$ and $s$.
If $r$ and $s$ are both odd, then $u^{r+s}\in\mathbb F_q^*$, whereas
$u^{r},u^{s}\in u\mathbb F_q^*$.
If $r$ is odd and $s$ is even, then $u^{s}\in\mathbb F_q^*$ is a nonzero
$\mathbb F_q$-component of $u^{r+s}+u^{r}+u^{s}$.
If $r$ is even and $s$ is odd, then $u^{r}\in\mathbb F_q^*$ is a nonzero
$\mathbb F_q$-component.
Finally, if $r$ and $s$ are both even, then
$
u^{r+s}+u^{r}+u^{s}\in\mathbb F_q.
$
In this last case the expression cannot belong to $u\mathbb F_q^*$.
Therefore, in all cases,
$
u^{r+s}+u^{r}+u^{s}\notin u\mathbb F_q^*.
$
Since $\alpha^a\in\mathbb F_q^*$, equation
\eqref{eq:trinomial-ratio-shifted} implies
$
\frac{Q(u^3)}{Q(u)}
\notin u\mathbb F_q^*.
$
head: environment

label: lem:single-run1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
After a cyclic shift, such a codeword would have support contained in
\[
\{0,1,\ldots,L-1\}
\]
for some $L\le7$. Its representative polynomial would therefore have
degree at most $L-1\le6$. Since every codeword polynomial of degree less
than $n$ is divisible by $g(x)$ and $\deg (g(x))=8$, this is impossible.
head: environment

label: lem:weight-five
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:weight-five}
There is no codeword $\mathbf{c}\in \mathcal{C}_2$ with
$
w_{\mathrm H}(\mathbf{c})=5
$
and with nonzero coordinates of both parities.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The two equations in \eqref{eq:parity-roots} imply that every nonzero
parity component contains at least two terms. Since the total Hamming
weight is five, one parity component is a binomial and the other is a
trinomial.

Assume first that $E$ is a trinomial and $O$ is a binomial. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:binomial-ratio-revised},
\[
\frac{O(u^3)}{O(u)}\in\mathbb F_q^*.
\]
The coupling identity \eqref{eq:coupling-ratio} would then imply
\[
\frac{E(u^3)}{E(u)}
=
u\frac{O(u^3)}{O(u)}
\in u\mathbb F_q^*,
\]
contradicting Lemma~\ref{lem:trinomial-ratio-revised}.
If $E$ is a binomial and $O$ is a trinomial, then
\[
\frac{O(u^3)}{O(u)}
=
u^{-1}\frac{E(u^3)}{E(u)}.
\]
Since
\[
u^{-1}=\alpha^{-1}u\in u\mathbb F_q^*,
\]
the right hand side belongs to $u\mathbb F_q^*$, again contradicting
Lemma~\ref{lem:trinomial-ratio-revised}.
head: environment

label: cor:weight-five-pair
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:weight-five-pair}
If $\mathbf{c}\in \mathcal{C}_2$ has Hamming weight five, then
\(
w_{p}(\mathbf{c})=10.
\)
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:weight-five}, all nonzero coordinates have the same
parity. Since $n$ is even, two coordinates of the same parity are never
cyclically adjacent. Hence every nonzero coordinate is a separate
nonzero run, and
\(
w_{p}(c)=2w_{\mathrm H}(c)=10.
\)
head: environment

label: thm:pair-distance-lower
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:pair-distance-lower}
For every odd prime power $q\ge7$ satisfying
$q\equiv3\pmod4$, the cyclic code defined by
\eqref{eq:gen-g3-revised} satisfies
\(
d_{p}(\mathcal{C}_2)\ge9.
\)
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $c\in \mathcal{C}_2$ be nonzero. By \eqref{eq:hamming-lower-bound},
\(
w_{\mathrm H}(c)\ge5.
\)
Suppose, for contradiction, that
\(
w_{p}(c)\le8.
\)
Since $n\ge24$, the support of $c$ is not the whole coordinate set. Hence
$
w_{p}(c)=w_{\mathrm H}(c)+\rho(c).
$

If $\rho(c)=1$, then
\(
w_{\mathrm H}(c)\le7,
\)
and Lemma~\ref{lem:single-run} gives a contradiction.
Therefore $\rho(c)\ge2$. It follows that
\(
w_{\mathrm H}(c)\le6.
\)
If $w_{\mathrm H}(c)=5$, then Corollary~\ref{cor:weight-five-pair}
gives
\(
w_{p}(c)=10,
\)
contradicting $w_{p}(c)\le8$.
Thus $w_{\mathrm H}(c)=6$. Since $\rho(c)\ge2$ and
$w_{p}(c)\le8$, we must have
\(
\rho(c)=2.
\)
The two cyclic runs therefore have lengths
\[
5+1,\qquad4+2,\qquad\text{or}\qquad3+3.
\]
All three patterns were excluded above.
This contradiction proves
\(
d_{p}(\mathcal{C}_2)\ge9.
\)
head: environment

label: thm:pair-distance-9-10
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:pair-distance-9-10}
For every odd prime power $q\ge7$ satisfying
$q\equiv3\pmod4$, the code $\mathcal{C}_2$ defined by
\eqref{eq:gen-g3-revised} has length
\(
n=4q-4,
\)
dimension
\(
\dim \mathcal{C}_2=4q-12,
\)
and minimum symbol-pair distance satisfying
\[
{9\le d_{p}(\mathcal{C}_2)\le10.}
\]
In particular, whenever $d_{p}(\mathcal{C}_2)=10$, the code is MDS in the
symbol-pair metric.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The length and dimension were established above. The lower bound follows
from Theorem~\ref{thm:pair-distance-lower}, while the upper bound is the
symbol-pair Singleton bound \eqref{eq:upper-bound}.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $q=31$ and write
$\mathbb F_{31^2}=\mathbb F_{31}(v)$, where $v^2=-1$.
Choose $\zeta=3+3v$,  by Magma, $\zeta$ has order $120$. And
the code $\mathcal{C}_2$ defined by (3) has generator polynomial
\[
g_{31}(x)
=x^8+9x^7+7x^6+22x^5+11x^4+3x^3+28x^2+28x+15
\]
and parameters $[120,112]_{31}$ with symbol-pair distance $d_p(\mathcal{C}_2)=9$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $q=7$ and write
$\mathbb F_{49}=\mathbb F_7(v)$, where $v^2=-1$. Choose $\zeta=1+v$,  by Magma, $\zeta$ has order $24$. And
the code $\mathcal{C}_2$ defined by (3) has generator polynomial
\[
g_7(x)
=x^8+2x^7+5x^6+5x^5+4x^4+3x^3+5x^2+4x+6
\]
and parameters $[24,16]_{7}$ with symbol-pair distance $d_p(\mathcal{C}_2)=10$.
head: environment

label: lem:basic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:basic}
The polynomial $g_\alpha(x)$ divides $x^n-1$ and has ten
distinct roots. Hence
\[
\dim_{\mathbb F_q}(\mathcal{C}_3)=n-10=2q-12.
\]
Moreover,
$
d_{\mathrm H}(\mathcal{C}_3)\ge8.
$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $q$ is odd and $\alpha$ is primitive,
$\alpha$ is a nonsquare in $\mathbb F_q$.
Choose $\beta\in\mathbb F_{q^2}$ with
$\beta^2=\alpha$. Then
\[
\beta^m=\alpha^{m/2}=-1,
\qquad
\operatorname{ord}(\beta)=2m=n,
\qquad
\beta^q=-\beta.
\]
The roots of $g_\alpha(x)$ are
$
1,\beta^2,\beta^4,\beta^6,
\pm\beta,\ \pm\beta^3,\ \pm\beta^5.
$
The first four are distinct elements of $\mathbb F_q$.
The remaining roots lie outside $\mathbb F_q$, since
their squares are odd powers of $\alpha$ and therefore
nonsquares.
Their constant terms $\alpha,\alpha^3,\alpha^5$ are
distinct because $\operatorname{ord}(\alpha)=m\ge10$.
Thus all ten roots are distinct. They are $n$-th roots
of unity, so  $g_\alpha(x)\mid x^n-1$.
The dimension follows from $\deg (g_\alpha(x))=10$.
Finally,
$
1,\beta,\beta^2,\ldots,\beta^6
$
are seven consecutive roots of $g_\alpha(x)$.
The BCH bound gives $d_{\mathrm H}(\mathcal{C}_3)\ge8$.
head: environment

label: lem:parity-count
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:parity-count}
Suppose that a support consists of cyclic runs of
total even length $L$. Let $r$ be the number of
odd length runs. Then $r$ is even, and the number
of even support positions lies between
\[
\frac{L-r}{2}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\frac{L+r}{2},
\]
inclusive.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $N_e$ denote the number of even indices in the support, and $N_o$ the number of odd indices in the support. Then $N_e + N_o = L$ is even. An even length segment contributes equally many even and odd positions, so $N_e - N_o$ equals the sum of contributions from all odd-length segments. Each odd length segment contributes either $+1$ or $-1$ to this difference. Since $N_e - N_o = L - 2N_o$ is even, the number $r$ of such segments must be even.
There are $r$ such segments in total. Each odd length segment can make $N_e$ exceed $N_o$ by at most $1$, or make $N_e$ fall below $N_o$ by at most $1$. Hence $-r \le N_e - N_o \le r$. Substitute $N_o = L - N_e$; then
$
-r \le N_e - (L - N_e) \le r,
$
and we thus obtain
\[
\frac{L - r}{2} \le N_e \le \frac{L + r}{2}.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:no-trinomial
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:no-trinomial}
Let
$
F(y)=\sum_{i=1}^3 f_i y^{u_i},
$
where $f_i\in\mathbb F_q^*$ and the exponents $u_i$
are distinct modulo $m$. Then $F$ cannot vanish
simultaneously at $\alpha,\alpha^3,\alpha^5$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed by contradiction. Assume that there exists a non zero polynomial \(F(y)\) such that
$F(\alpha)=F(\alpha^3)=F(\alpha^5)=0.$
Set
$
z_i=\alpha^{2u_i},
b_i=f_i\alpha^{u_i},
$ since $f_i\in\mathbb F_q^*$ and $\alpha\neq0$, all $b_i\neq0$.
The three vanishing equations give


\[
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1&1\\
z_1&z_2&z_3\\
z_1^2&z_2^2&z_3^2
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}b_1\\b_2\\b_3\end{pmatrix}=0.
\]
If the \(z_i\) are distinct, the matrix is invertible, the system of equations has only the trivial solution.
If exactly two of the \(z_i\) coincide, the coefficient of
the remaining column must be zero. Both cases
contradict $b_1b_2b_3\ne0$.
All three  \(z_i\) cannot coincide because each residue class
modulo $m/2$ contains only two residue classes modulo
$m$, whereas the $u_i$ are distinct modulo $m$.
head: environment

label: lem:frobenius-eight
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:frobenius-eight}
Let $\mathbf{c}\in \mathcal{C}_3$ have Hamming weight eight, with
four support positions of each parity. Define
\[
\mathcal E=\{\beta^s:s\in\operatorname{supp}(\mathbf{c}),\
s\text{ even}\},
\]
\[
\mathcal O=\{\beta^s:s\in\operatorname{supp}(\mathbf{c}),\
s\text{ odd}\},
\]
and
\[
A(z)=\prod_{e\in\mathcal E}(z-e)
=z^4-e_1z^3+e_2z^2-e_3z+e_4,
\]
\[
B(z)=\prod_{o\in\mathcal O}(z-o)
=z^4-o_1z^3+o_2z^2-o_3z+o_4.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:symmetric-constraints}
e_2=o_2,\qquad
e_4=o_4,\qquad
e_1o_3=e_3o_1.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $H(z)=A(z)B(z)$. The codeword satisfies the root condition, so we have
\[
c(\beta^j)=0,\qquad 0\le j\le6,
\]
which forms  a $7\times8$ Vandermonde system with a
1-dimensional kernel. The standard interpolation
identity gives a kernel generator
$
\left(H'(\beta^s)^{-1}\right)_
{s\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}.
$
Thus, for some $\lambda\in\mathbb F_{q^2}^*$,
\[
c_s=\frac{\lambda}{H'(\beta^s)}.
\]
Since $c_s\in\mathbb F_q^*$, so
$
H'(\beta^s)^q=K H'(\beta^s),$ where $
K=\lambda^q/\lambda.
$


For each root $e\in E$ of $A(z)$, we have $e^q = e$. and for each root $o\in O$ of $B(z)$, we have $o^q = -o$.
Evaluate the identity $\big(H'(\gamma)\big)^q = K H'(\gamma)$ at the roots of $A(z)$ and $B(z)$.
For any $e\in E$, $H'(e)=A'(e)B(e)$. Since $A'(e)\neq 0$ and $A'(e)^q=A'(e)$, we obtain
$
B(e)^q = K B(e).
$
Using $B(e)^q = B(-e)$, we get $B(-e)-K B(e)=0$ for all four roots $e$ of $A(z)$.
Hence $B(-z)-K B(z)$ is divisible by $A(z)$. Comparing leading coefficients,
\[
B(-z)-K B(z) = (1-K)A(z).
\]
By the same argument, we get
$
A(-z)+K A(z) = (1+K)B(z).
$
The coefficients of $z^2$ and the constant terms
give $e_2=o_2$ and $e_4=o_4$, since the characteristic
is odd. The coefficients of $z^3$ and $z$ give
\[
(1-K)e_j+(1+K)o_j=0,\qquad j=1,3.
\]
Because $(1-K,1+K)\ne(0,0)$, the vectors
$(e_1,o_1)$ and $(e_3,o_3)$ are linearly dependent.
This proves the last identity.
head: environment

label: thm:interval
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:interval}
Let $q\ge11$. Then
$\dim (\mathcal{C}_3)=2q-12,
$ and
$11\le d_{p}(\mathcal{C}_3)\le12.
$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The dimension follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:basic}.
The Singleton bound for symbol-pair codes gives
\[
d_{p}(\mathcal{C}_3)
\le n-\dim (\mathcal{C}_3)+2=12.
\]

Suppose that a nonzero word satisfies
$w_{p}(\mathbf{c})\le10$. Since $n\ge20$, its support
is proper. By $d_{\mathrm H}(\mathcal{C}_3)\ge8$ and
$wt_p(\mathbf{c})=w_H{(\mathbf{c})}+\rho(\mathbf{c})
$, we have
$
(w_{\mathrm H}(\mathbf{c}),\rho(\mathbf{c}))
\in\{(8,1),(8,2),(9,1)\}.
$
A one-run word of length at most nine can be shifted
to a nonzero polynomial of degree at most eight.
Such a polynomial cannot be divisible by
$g_\alpha$, which has degree ten.

It remains to exclude $(8,2)$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:parity-count}, the parity counts are
$(3,5)$, $(4,4)$, or $(5,3)$. The first and last
possibilities contradict Lemma~\ref{lem:no-trinomial}.
Thus the split is $(4,4)$.
After a cyclic shift, write the support as
\[
S=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}
\cup\{t,\ldots,t+7-a\},
\qquad 1\le a\le4,
\]
with both cyclic gaps nonempty.
From the conclusion of Lemma ~\ref{lem:frobenius-eight}, \(e_4=o_4\). Recall that
\[e_4=\prod_{s\in S_{\text{even}}}\beta^s=\beta^{\sum_{s\in S_{\text{even}}}s},\qquad
o_4=\prod_{s\in S_{\text{odd}}}\beta^s=\beta^{\sum_{s\in S_{\text{odd}}}s}.\]
Equating them yields
\(\beta^{\sum_{s\in S_{\text{even}}}s-\sum_{s\in S_{\text{odd}}}s}=1.\)
Since \(\beta\) has order n, we obtain \(n\mid \Delta\), where
\(\Delta=\sum_{s\in S_{\text{even}}}s-\sum_{s\in S_{\text{odd}}}s.\)




The cases compatible with the parity split $(4,4)$
are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
a&\text{parity of }t&\Delta\\ \hline
1&\text{odd}&-(t+3)\\
2&\text{even}&-4\\
2&\text{odd}&2\\
3&\text{odd}&-(t+1)\\
4&\text{even}&-4\\
4&\text{odd}&0
\end{array}
\]
The nonempty-gap conditions imply
$0<|\Delta|<n$ in every row except the last.
Hence $a=4$ and $t=2s+1$.

For this remaining case,
\[
\mathcal E=\{1,\alpha,\alpha^{s+1},\alpha^{s+2}\},
\]
\[
\mathcal O
=\{\beta,\beta\alpha,\beta\alpha^s,\beta\alpha^{s+1}\}.
\]
By Lemma ~\ref{lem:frobenius-eight}, expanding $e_2-o_2$ gives
\[
e_2-o_2
=\alpha(\alpha-1)(\alpha^{2s+1}-1)=0.
\]
Thus $m\mid2s+1$, which is impossible because $m$
is even. This excludes every pair weight at most
ten.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $q=19$ and choose $\alpha=3\in\mathbb F_{19}^{*}$,
which has order $18$.
The code $\mathcal{C}_3$ has generator polynomial
\[
\begin{aligned}
g_\alpha(x)={}&x^{10}+17x^9+3x^8+17x^7+12x^6+18x^4+14x^3+3x^2+3x+7
\end{aligned}
\]
and parameters $[36,26]_{19}$ with symbol-pair distance
$d_p(\mathcal{C}_3)=11$.

title: Example
body_md:
Let $q=11$ and choose $\alpha=2\in\mathbb F_{11}^{*}$,
which has order $10$.
The code $\mathcal{C}_3$ has generator polynomial
\[
\begin{aligned}
g_\alpha(x)={}&x^{10}+7x^9+6x^8+4x^7+x^6+3x^4+8x^3+8x^2+5x+1
\end{aligned}
\]
and parameters $[20,10]_{11}$ with symbol-pair distance
$d_p(\mathcal{C}_3)=12$.
